patient.name: Sophie Hartley
patient.complaint: Blurred, painful vision in the right eye for 4 days
background: Scandinavian mother; grew up in Scotland
Two years ago: 'pins and needles' up both legs for 3 weeks, settled alone
Graphic designer in Hackney; no regular medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' in a young woman with two neurological episodes in different places at different times: optic neuritis, INO, Lhermitte's sign or a sensory level. Distractors are GBS, B12 deficiency, stroke and myasthenia.

points: Sophie, 28: right eye blurred for 4 days.
**Pain on moving the eye**; colours look 'washed out'.
Two years ago: tingling legs for 3 weeks, fully recovered.
No headache, fever or weakness now.

steps.lead: Two episodes, two different CNS sites (optic nerve, then spinal cord), two years apart: that is **dissemination in time and space**, the core of MS.
Sophie ticks the risk boxes: **woman aged 20 to 40**, Northern European ancestry and previous **EBV**. Attacks that recover fully fit **relapsing-remitting MS**.

points: Red appears 'pink' to the right eye (colour desaturation).
Swinging light: right pupil **dilates** when the light reaches it.
Fundoscopy: right disc looks normal (retrobulbar neuritis).

steps.q: The right pupil dilates when the torch swings from left to right. What is this sign?
steps.r: A **RAPD** means the right optic nerve carries less light signal: the hallmark of **optic neuritis**.

steps.lead: Sophie has the commonest MS presentation, **optic neuritis**: pain on eye movement, reduced acuity, colour desaturation and a RAPD. The disc may look normal early and pale later.

steps.title: Optic neuritis or something else?
head: Feature
Optic neuritis (MS)
Distractor
rows: Giant cell arteritis: jaw claudication, headache, age >50
Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden, painless
Acute glaucoma: fixed mid-dilated, red eye
Papilloedema: swollen discs, both eyes, acuity kept

points: On direct questions she adds more:
Electric shocks down her arms when she **bends her neck**.
Looking left: right eye does not adduct; left eye flickers.

steps.title: Signs that shout MS
nodes: Optic neuritis: painful vision loss, RAPD
Lhermitte's sign: shocks on neck flexion
INO: failed adduction, nystagmus of abducting eye
Transverse myelitis, ataxia, new urinary symptoms
steps.caption: Any one plus a second episode elsewhere in time should make you think MS.

steps.lead: Her neurologist uses the **McDonald criteria**. Sophie is relapsing-remitting; a steady decline with no relapses would point to **primary progressive** MS.

steps.text: Do not pick MS for a **peripheral** picture: absent reflexes, glove-and-stocking loss or an ascending paralysis after infection point to neuropathy or GBS. MS is a **CNS** (UMN) disease.

steps.lead: Sophie's outlook is better than average: young, **female**, sensory and visual onset. Motor onset, male sex, older age and many MRI lesions predict worse disability.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast) or 'Which CSF finding is most likely?' (oligoclonal bands).

steps.q: Sophie has optic neuritis and an old spinal episode. Which test best confirms MS?
o: MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast
steps.r: **MRI with gadolinium** shows plaques and proves dissemination in time and space. CT misses demyelination.

steps.lead: Because Sophie presented with optic neuritis, she has an **urgent MRI brain with contrast** to look for central plaques. LP is the supporting test.

points: One plaque **enhances** with gadolinium; others do not.
A further plaque in the cervical cord.

steps.lead: An **enhancing** (new) plus a **non-enhancing** (old) plaque on one scan shows dissemination in time; brain plus cord shows dissemination in space.

steps.title: Sophie's lumbar puncture
rows: Present in CSF, absent in serum
steps.text: Bands only in the CSF mean IgG is being made **inside the CNS**: immune activity typical of MS.

visual.title: CSF white cell count
bands: Mild rise: MS can do this
visual.label: Sophie 4
visual.caption: MS CSF is usually bland: normal or mildly raised cells. A big pleocytosis points away from MS.

steps.text: **Oligoclonal bands** support MS but are not specific. They must be in CSF and **not** matched in serum.

points: Five years later: a relapse leaves Sophie with urgency and dribbling.
She cannot tell whether her bladder empties fully.

steps.lead: For MS bladder symptoms, start with a **bladder ultrasound** and post-void residual: a large residual means she needs intermittent self-catheterisation.

steps.text: A normal **CT head** is not reassurance: CT cannot see demyelinating plaques. The answer for suspected MS is always **MRI**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' for a relapse (high-dose methylprednisolone, IV for optic neuritis) and long-term choices: disease-modifying therapy, baclofen for spasticity.

steps.q: Sophie has acute optic neuritis with significant visual loss. What is the initial treatment?
steps.r: High-dose **IV methylprednisolone** speeds recovery of a relapse. DMTs prevent future relapses; they do not treat this one.

steps.lead: Sophie gets **IV methylprednisolone** for her optic neuritis. A later non-visual relapse would usually be **high-dose oral methylprednisolone**, agreed with the MS team.

steps.text: Steroids shorten a relapse but **do not change long-term disability**. Never choose them as long-term disease modification.

visual.title: Right visual acuity (letters read on chart)
visual.caption: Vision recovers over weeks after steroids. A relapse that settles is the 'remitting' in relapsing-remitting.

steps.title: Long-term plan for RRMS
nodes: Start a DMT: interferon beta or ocrelizumab
steps.caption: DMTs reduce relapse rate; symptom drugs make daily life easier.

points: Over 3 years Sophie has **3 relapses a year** despite interferon.
She now has stiff legs that spasm at night.

steps.lead: Sophie's highly active disease means **natalizumab**. Her stiff, spasming legs need **baclofen** (or gabapentin) with physiotherapy.

steps.title: Which drug for which job?
head: Drug
Job in MS
rows: First-line DMT: fewer relapses (patients who walk unaided)
Highly active RRMS or failure of first-line DMT

steps.lead: Sophie's care follows **NICE NG220** (MS in adults) and her diagnosis rests on the **McDonald criteria**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the mechanism of MS (T-cell attack on oligodendrocyte myelin), which structure causes INO (MLF), why heat worsens symptoms, or how natalizumab works.

steps.title: How a plaque forms
steps.caption: Symptoms depend on where the plaque sits.

steps.lead: Sophie's plaques in the optic nerve and cervical cord explain her two different relapses: same disease, **different site**.

steps.q: Which cell makes the myelin that is damaged in MS?
steps.r: **Oligodendrocytes** myelinate the CNS. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves, which is why GBS is peripheral and MS is central.

steps.lead: Sophie's vision blurring after a **hot shower** is Uhthoff's phenomenon: heat further slows conduction in already demyelinated fibres.

visual.title: Uhthoff's phenomenon: symptoms with body temperature
visual.caption: The blur rises and falls with temperature: transient, not a new relapse.

steps.lead: Sophie's right eye failing to adduct on left gaze, with nystagmus in the abducting left eye, localises a **right MLF** lesion: a right INO.

steps.text: INO is named for the eye that **cannot adduct**; that is the side of the MLF lesion. A **bilateral** INO in a young adult is almost always MS.

steps.lead: Each relapse leaves a little damage. Over years, **axonal loss** builds up, which is why disability becomes permanent.
Natalizumab blocks the adhesion molecule (**α4-integrin**) T cells use to cross into the brain, so fewer reach Sophie's CNS.

steps.text: Natalizumab carries a risk of **PML** (JC virus). Exams may ask which infection to monitor for on natalizumab.

mcq.q: Which is the most common presenting feature of MS?
mcq.r: **Optic neuritis** is the commonest first presentation.

mcq.q: What two things must be shown to diagnose MS?
mcq.r: Lesions at **different times** and in **different places** in the CNS (McDonald criteria).

o: Electric shocks down limbs on neck flexion
Pupil dilating on swinging light test
mcq.r: **Lhermitte's**: tingling or shocks on neck flexion from a cervical cord lesion. Heat worsening is Uhthoff's.

mcq.q: Which MS course is the most common?
mcq.r: **Relapsing-remitting** is most common; primary progressive has steady decline without relapses.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for MS?
o: MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast
mcq.r: **MRI with gadolinium** shows periventricular plaques and dissemination in time and space.
**Oligoclonal IgG bands** in CSF (not serum). Albuminocytological dissociation is GBS.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for an acute MS relapse with optic neuritis?
mcq.r: **IV methylprednisolone** for optic neuritis; DMTs prevent future relapses.

mcq.q: Which drug treats spasticity in MS?

o: Blocks leukocyte adhesion so lymphocytes cannot cross the BBB
mcq.r: It blocks **α4-integrin** adhesion, keeping lymphocytes out of the CNS.

mcq.q: Which structure is damaged in internuclear ophthalmoplegia?
mcq.r: The **MLF** links the abducens and oculomotor nuclei for conjugate horizontal gaze.

prompts.q: What is MS and what two things are needed to diagnose it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one episode is not MS; look for two CNS sites at two times.

points.p: Autoimmune T-cell attack on CNS myelin (oligodendrocytes)
points.why: Peripheral myelin (Schwann cells) is GBS, not MS.
Lesions at different times, e.g. enhancing and non-enhancing on one MRI.
The named criteria for diagnosing MS.

prompts.q: Who typically gets MS, and what is the most common course?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem is usually a young woman.

points.why: Prevalence rises with distance from the equator.
EBV is the strongest environmental association.
Primary progressive is steady decline without relapses.

prompts.q: What are the features of optic neuritis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the most common MS presentation. Painful + RAPD + colour loss.

points.why: Colour loss is out of proportion to acuity loss.
Seen on the swinging light test.

points.p: Disc normal early, pale (optic atrophy) later
points.why: Retrobulbar neuritis gives a normal disc initially.

prompts.q: Name other classic MS signs apart from optic neuritis.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each sign is a lesion in a different place; two sites = MS.

points.why: Failed adduction, nystagmus in the abducting eye.

points.p: Lhermitte's sign: shocks on neck flexion

prompts.q: What are the complications and the poor prognostic factors in MS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: men and motor onset do worse.

points.why: Men have a worse prognosis overall.

points.p: Motor signs at onset, early relapses
points.why: Sensory or optic onset does better.

prompts.q: What is the gold-standard test for MS and what does it show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: always MRI, never CT.

points.p: MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast (gadolinium)
Enhancing + non-enhancing lesions = dissemination in time
Lesions in different sites = dissemination in space

prompts.q: Which other tests help in MS and what do they show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: LP supports; ultrasound for the bladder.

points.why: Bands in CSF but not serum.

points.p: Urgent MRI brain with contrast after optic neuritis
Bladder ultrasound / post-void residual first for bladder symptoms

prompts.q: How do you treat an acute MS relapse?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: steroids treat the attack; they do not change the long-term course.

points.p: Steroids do not change long-term disability
points.why: Never pick steroids as a DMT.

prompts.q: What long-term treatments are used in MS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: DMTs for relapse rate, symptom drugs for spasticity.

points.p: Interferon beta: fewer relapses in RRMS (walking unaided)
Natalizumab: highly active RRMS (>2 relapses/yr) or first-line failure

points.why: Plus muscle relaxants and pain management.

prompts.q: Why does a plaque cause symptoms, and why does heat make them worse?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain the finding in the vignette from first principles.

points.p: T cells cross the BBB and strip oligodendrocyte myelin
Demyelination slows or blocks saltatory conduction
points.why: Symptoms depend on the plaque site.

points.p: Heat further slows conduction in demyelinated axons
Repeated attacks cause axonal loss and permanent disability

prompts.q: What causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and how does natalizumab work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: localise to the MLF; name the drug's target.

points.p: Lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus
points.why: It links the CN VI and CN III nuclei.

points.p: Impaired adduction of affected eye, nystagmus of abducting eye
points.why: Named by the eye that cannot adduct.

glossary.MS: Multiple sclerosis: autoimmune demyelination of the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.Oligodendrocytes: Cells that make myelin in the central nervous system.
glossary.Demyelination: Loss of the fatty myelin sheath around nerve fibres, slowing or blocking conduction.
glossary.Dissemination in time and space: Lesions occurring at different times and in different parts of the CNS; required to diagnose MS.
glossary.McDonald criteria: The clinical and MRI rules used to diagnose MS.
glossary.Relapsing-remitting: MS course with attacks followed by partial or full recovery; the commonest form.
glossary.Primary progressive: MS that worsens steadily from onset with no discrete relapses.
glossary.Secondary progressive: MS that becomes steadily progressive after a relapsing-remitting phase.
glossary.Optic neuritis: Inflammation of the optic nerve: painful eye movement, reduced acuity and colour vision.
glossary.RAPD: Relative afferent pupillary defect: the pupil dilates when light swings to the eye with the damaged optic nerve.
glossary.relative afferent pupillary defect: Pupil dilates when light swings to the affected eye, showing optic nerve damage.
glossary.Colour desaturation: Colours, especially red, look faded in one eye; an early sign of optic nerve disease.
glossary.Optic atrophy: A pale optic disc from lost optic nerve fibres after damage.
glossary.Retrobulbar neuritis: Optic neuritis behind the eye, so the disc looks normal at first.
glossary.Transverse myelitis: Inflammation across a segment of spinal cord, giving a sensory level, weakness and bladder problems.
glossary.Sensory level: A horizontal line on the trunk below which sensation is reduced; points to a spinal cord lesion.
glossary.INO: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: failed adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the other on lateral gaze.
glossary.Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: Eye movement sign from an MLF lesion: affected eye cannot adduct, the other eye has nystagmus.
glossary.MLF: Medial longitudinal fasciculus: brainstem tract linking the CN VI and CN III nuclei for conjugate gaze.
glossary.Medial longitudinal fasciculus: Brainstem tract coordinating horizontal eye movements between the two eyes.
glossary.Nystagmus: Involuntary rhythmic jerking of the eyes.
glossary.Uhthoff's phenomenon: Temporary worsening of MS symptoms with heat, such as a hot bath or exercise.
glossary.Lhermitte's sign: Electric shock sensation down the spine or limbs on neck flexion; a cervical cord lesion.
glossary.Spasticity: Velocity-dependent increased tone from an upper motor neurone lesion.
glossary.Ataxia: Unsteady, poorly coordinated movement, often from a cerebellar lesion.
glossary.EBV: Epstein-Barr virus, the cause of glandular fever; a strong risk factor for MS.
glossary.Oligoclonal bands: Distinct IgG bands in CSF but not serum, showing antibody made inside the CNS.
glossary.Gadolinium: MRI contrast agent; enhancing lesions are new and active.
glossary.Periventricular: Next to the brain's ventricles; the classic site of MS plaques.
glossary.Plaque: A focal area of demyelination seen on MRI as a bright T2 lesion.
glossary.T2 hyperintensity: A bright area on a T2-weighted MRI, as seen with MS plaques.
glossary.Post-void residual: Urine left in the bladder after voiding, measured by ultrasound.
glossary.Methylprednisolone: High-dose corticosteroid used to shorten MS relapses.
glossary.DMT: Disease-modifying therapy: a drug that reduces relapse rate in MS.
glossary.Interferon beta: Injected first-line disease-modifying therapy that reduces MS relapses.
glossary.Natalizumab: Monoclonal antibody against α4-integrin that stops lymphocytes entering the CNS; used in highly active MS.
glossary.Ocrelizumab: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B cells; a disease-modifying therapy for MS.
glossary.Baclofen: GABA-B agonist muscle relaxant used for spasticity.
glossary.Gabapentin: Drug used for neuropathic pain and spasticity in MS.
glossary.Gastrostomy: Feeding tube placed through the abdominal wall into the stomach.
glossary.Saltatory conduction: Fast nerve conduction where impulses jump between nodes of Ranvier on myelinated axons.
glossary.Blood-brain barrier: Tight endothelial barrier controlling entry of cells and molecules into the brain.
glossary.PML: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: JC virus brain infection; a risk of natalizumab.
glossary.Axonal loss: Death of nerve fibres after repeated demyelination; causes permanent disability.
glossary.NG220: NICE guideline on multiple sclerosis in adults.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 5 day history of blurred vision in her left eye with pain on eye movement. A year ago she had numbness of her right leg for a month that resolved. Visual acuity is 6/24 in the left eye with reduced colour vision. There is a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question. Look for a pattern across time, not just today's symptom.

clues: numbness of her right leg for a month that resolved
steps.x: Young woman; painful vision loss with colour desaturation and RAPD = **optic neuritis**; a previous resolved episode elsewhere = **dissemination in time and space**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Optic neuritis plus a past different CNS episode: **multiple sclerosis**.

elim: CRAO is sudden and painless, with a cherry-red spot on fundoscopy.
Myasthenia causes fatigable ptosis and diplopia; acuity and pupils are normal.
Detachment is painless, with flashes, floaters and a curtain, without pain on eye movement.
Temporal (giant cell) arteritis affects over-50s with headache and jaw claudication.

steps.x: **B. Multiple sclerosis.** Two CNS episodes, different sites, different times = MS. Normal fundoscopy fits retrobulbar neuritis.

technique.stem: A 32 year old woman has a 1 week history of tingling in both legs and electric shock sensations down her back when she bends her neck. Two years ago she had an episode of double vision that resolved over 6 weeks. She has brisk reflexes in both legs and an upgoing left plantar.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast

steps.x: It asks for the **diagnostic** test, so pick the gold standard, not a supporting test.

clues: electric shock sensations down her back when she bends her neck
steps.x: Lhermitte's sign (cervical cord) plus an old resolved diplopia (brainstem) and UMN signs: suspected **MS**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gold standard for MS: **MRI brain and spinal cord with gadolinium**.

elim: CT cannot reliably show demyelinating plaques.
LP (oligoclonal bands) supports the diagnosis but does not show dissemination in space and time.
Nerve conduction tests peripheral nerves; brisk reflexes and an upgoing plantar are central.
B12 deficiency is reasonable to exclude but gives absent ankle jerks and does not explain past diplopia or Lhermitte's.

steps.x: **C. MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast.** Suspected MS = MRI with contrast. LP is second, supportive.

technique.stem: A 30 year old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis has a 3 day history of painful loss of vision in her right eye. Visual acuity is 6/60 in the right eye. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. She is otherwise well.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of an **acute relapse**: treat the attack now.
Known RRMS with optic neuritis causing marked visual loss: an **acute relapse**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute optic neuritis relapse: **IV methylprednisolone**.

elim: Natalizumab is a DMT to reduce future relapses, not to treat this one.
There is no infection; aciclovir has no role.
Baclofen treats spasticity.
Plasma exchange is for steroid-refractory relapses or GBS and myasthenic crisis, not first-line.

steps.x: **A. IV methylprednisolone.** Relapse = steroids; prevention = DMT.

technique.stem: A 26 year old woman has double vision on looking to the left. On examination, on left gaze her right eye does not move past the midline and her left eye shows horizontal nystagmus. Convergence is normal. MRI shows multiple periventricular white matter lesions.
technique.q: Which structure is most likely to be affected?

steps.x: It asks for the anatomical structure, so localise the eye movement sign.

clues: her right eye does not move past the midline
steps.x: Failed adduction on lateral gaze with nystagmus of the abducting eye and preserved convergence = **INO**; plaques = MS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: INO from an MLF lesion on the side of the eye that cannot adduct: **right MLF**.

elim: A left CN VI palsy stops the left eye abducting; here the left eye abducts.
The lesion is on the side of the eye that fails to adduct: the right.
Chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia, not eye movement problems.
A CN III palsy would affect convergence too, with ptosis and a dilated pupil.

steps.x: **D. Right medial longitudinal fasciculus.** Name the MLF on the side of the non-adducting eye.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 1 week history of blurred vision in her right eye. It hurts when she moves the eye. Eighteen months ago she had numbness from her waist down that resolved over 6 weeks. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Painful monocular vision loss with a RAPD is optic neuritis; with an earlier resolved spinal cord episode this is dissemination in time and space, so MS. GBS is a peripheral disease.

steps.x: Diagnosis: link today's eye to the past episode.

clues: hurts when she moves the eye
numbness from her waist down that resolved
steps.x: Optic neuritis now, a resolved sensory level (transverse myelitis) before: two CNS sites, two times.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Multiple sclerosis**.

elim: Glaucoma gives a red eye, halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
A pituitary tumour gives slow, painless bitemporal field loss.
Detachment is painless, with flashes, floaters and a curtain.
Temporal arteritis is in over-50s with headache and raised ESR.

steps.x: **B. Multiple sclerosis.** Optic neuritis + previous myelitis in a young woman = MS.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 2 week history of tingling in her hands. She notices an electric shock feeling running down her spine and into her legs whenever she bends her head forward. Three years ago she had an episode of unsteadiness that settled. Reflexes are brisk in all four limbs.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Lhermitte's sign with UMN signs and a previous resolved cerebellar episode shows dissemination in time and space, so MS. GBS and B12 deficiency reduce reflexes.

steps.x: Diagnosis: name the sign, then put the episodes together.

clues: electric shock feeling running down her spine
whenever she bends her head forward
steps.x: **Lhermitte's sign** (cervical cord lesion), a prior cerebellar episode, UMN signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Relapsing CNS disease with Lhermitte's: **MS**.

elim: Spondylosis is in older adults and does not explain the earlier cerebellar episode.
GBS causes areflexia, not brisk reflexes.
A syrinx is slowly progressive with cape-like loss of pain and temperature, not relapsing.
B12 deficiency usually gives absent ankle jerks and is not relapsing.

steps.x: **C. Multiple sclerosis.** Lhermitte's in a young adult with a past episode = MS.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman with multiple sclerosis has difficulty seeing on looking to the right. On examination, on right gaze her left eye fails to adduct and her right eye has nystagmus. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding?
practice.e: Failure of adduction of the left eye with nystagmus in the abducting right eye is a left INO from a left MLF plaque. A right INO would affect the right eye's adduction.

steps.x: It asks you to name the eye movement sign and its side.
Failed adduction with nystagmus of the abducting eye = **INO**; side = the eye that fails to adduct.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left INO** (left MLF lesion).

elim: That is a chiasmal lesion, a visual field sign.
A left CN VI palsy would stop left eye abduction.
INO is named by the eye that fails to adduct: the left.
A CN III palsy causes ptosis, a 'down and out' eye and a dilated pupil.

steps.x: **B. Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia.** Name INO by the eye that cannot adduct.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. She reports that her vision becomes blurred and her legs feel weaker after a hot bath or exercise, and settles within an hour of cooling down. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Examination is unchanged from her last clinic visit.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
practice.e: Transient worsening with heat that resolves on cooling, with an unchanged examination, is Uhthoff's phenomenon. A true relapse lasts over 24 hours without fever.

steps.x: It asks for an explanation of a transient symptom.

clues: after a hot bath or exercise
settles within an hour of cooling down
steps.x: Heat-triggered, short-lived worsening with no new signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Uhthoff's phenomenon**: heat slows conduction in demyelinated fibres.

elim: Lhermitte's is shocks on neck flexion.
A relapse lasts more than 24 hours and does not settle on cooling.
Atrophy is permanent; this is transient.
She is not on long-term steroids and the weakness settles in an hour.

steps.x: **E. Uhthoff's phenomenon.** Heat-triggered and brief = Uhthoff's, not a relapse.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has a 4 year history of gradually worsening stiffness and weakness of both legs. There have been no discrete attacks or periods of improvement. He now walks with a stick. Both legs are spastic with brisk reflexes. MRI shows multiple spinal cord and periventricular white matter lesions. CSF shows oligoclonal bands.
practice.q: Which is the most likely type of multiple sclerosis?
practice.e: Steady decline from onset without relapses is primary progressive MS, which presents later and equally in men. Secondary progressive MS follows earlier relapsing-remitting disease.

steps.x: It asks for the subtype, so read the shape of the history.

clues: no discrete attacks or periods of improvement
steps.x: Steady progression from onset with no relapses, in an older man.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Primary progressive MS**.

elim: Benign MS means little disability after many years; he already needs a stick.
CIS is one single episode, not 4 years of decline.
RRMS has discrete relapses with recovery between them.
SPMS follows a period of relapsing-remitting disease; he never had relapses.

steps.x: **C. Primary progressive.** Monophasic steady decline from the start = primary progressive.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 10 day history of numbness from her umbilicus downwards and difficulty passing urine. Two years ago she had painful blurred vision in her left eye that recovered. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. There is a sensory level at T10 with brisk lower limb reflexes.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Transverse myelitis with new urinary symptoms after a previous optic neuritis shows dissemination in time and space, so MS. Cauda equina gives LMN signs and no sensory level.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a cord syndrome in a young woman. Look back in time.

clues: painful blurred vision in her left eye that recovered
steps.x: Acute transverse myelitis now (sensory level, bladder, UMN signs); past optic neuritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MS**: optic neuritis then transverse myelitis.

elim: Cauda equina is a LMN lesion: reduced reflexes and saddle anaesthesia, no sensory level.
GBS has no sensory level and causes areflexia.
Metastatic compression is in older patients with known cancer and back pain.
An abscess gives fever and severe back pain.

steps.x: **C. Multiple sclerosis.** Transverse myelitis + past optic neuritis = MS.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 3 day history of painful loss of vision in her left eye. Visual acuity is 6/36 in the left eye with a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy is normal. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to look for central demyelination?
practice.e: After optic neuritis, an urgent contrast MRI brain looks for central white matter plaques that predict MS. LP adds oligoclonal bands but cannot show where lesions are.

steps.x: It asks how to find **central demyelination**, which is imaging.
Optic neuritis: the question is whether there are other plaques (dissemination in space).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent **MRI brain with contrast**.

elim: CT does not show demyelinating plaques.
ESR is for GCA in older patients.
LP supports MS but does not look for plaques.
Fields describe the defect but do not show central lesions.

steps.x: **D. MRI brain with contrast.** Optic neuritis → urgent MRI brain with contrast.
